passages: Google DeepMind's AlphaProof system is a language model trained to write Lean code; it autonomously performed at silver medal standard on the 2024 IMO, and things are moving very fast in this domain.

Nowadays the work of many Fields Medallists have been formalized, mostly in the Lean theorem prover; examples include the Clausen—Scholze theory of liquid modules and the Gowers—Green—Manners—Tao proof of the polynomial Freiman—Ruzsa conjecture.

passages: In mathematics, these technologies have been applied to solve olympiad-style problems at the level of an International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) Silver Medal Reference 33 and will no doubt surpass us soon.

On the other hand, Deepmind’s 2024 Silver Medal performance uses a specialized algorithm AlphaGeometry2 to solve geometry problems, and for other problems, they appear⁠Footnote5 to use a combination of the above strategies together with a reinforced learning algorithm styled after AlphaZero Reference 77.

The potential of autoformalization has already been evidenced by Numina’s winning performance Reference 62 in the AI Mathematical Olympiad (AIMO) progress prize Reference 17 and Deepmind’s performance on the 2024 IMO deserving of a Silver Medal.

The search space for proof generation, however, is vastly larger than for most games raising major theoretical and engineering challenges, some of which have presumably been solved by AlphaProof, Numina, DeepSeek, and the various other teams specializing in autoformalization.

items.meta_description: [This is a guest post by Thomas Hales. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] Mathematicians have been weighing in on what they value ab…
passages: Dan Selsam has contributed to Lean from its early days and was one of the creators of the IMO grand challenge aimed at achieving IMO-level problem solving verified in Lean.
PolymathAnonymous on Even more posts, opinion piece…Xianghao Tang on Lean Grimoireecstatic6d274314ad on Even more posts, opinion piece…jmdpark on G.R.H.
Among mathematicians, the Lean theorem prover is the most popular, and this post will focus on Lean.
Lean proofs should never be believed until they have been checked by the kernel.

For instance, for Navier-Stokes, a human should check that the statement in Lean corresponds with Fefferman’s statement of the Millennium Prize Problem, and specifically that concepts such as the field of real numbers, partial derivatives, and measure are correctly defined in Lean.
Develop other Lean kernels, and cross-check formal proofs.

My overall assessment is that our theoretical understanding of Lean’s type theory is not what we would like it to be and that the mathematical community as a whole is giving short shrift to very important type-theoretic questions related to Lean.
I think if someone writes a paper, they maybe cannot say “here’s a proof that X is true, and an ai generated lean formalization showing my approach is correct!!”
